items.followUp: Differentiate between n-type and p-type semiconductors.

rubric.why: A donor atom supplies an extra electron to the semiconductor.
rubric.description: States what a donor atom does.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the donor as an impurity that donates an electron, usually a pentavalent atom.

rubric.why: An acceptor atom accepts an electron, leaving a hole.
rubric.description: States what an acceptor atom does.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the acceptor as an impurity that accepts an electron and creates a hole, usually a trivalent atom.

modelAnswer: A donor atom is an impurity atom, usually pentavalent, that donates an extra electron to the semiconductor and produces n-type material.
An acceptor atom is an impurity atom, usually trivalent, that accepts an electron and creates a hole, producing p-type material.

items.followUp: Write down any two physical properties of non-metals.

rubric.description: Gives one correct property of metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid property, such as malleability, ductility or good electrical and thermal conductivity.

rubric.why: A second distinct correct property is required.
rubric.description: Gives a second correct property of metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a further valid property distinct from the first.

modelAnswer: Metals are malleable; they can be beaten into sheets.
Metals are good conductors of heat and electricity.

items.followUp: Give two differences between crystalline and amorphous solids.

rubric.why: Crystalline solids have an orderly particle arrangement and a definite melting point.
rubric.description: States a structural or melting-point distinction for crystalline solids.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the regular arrangement and sharp melting point of crystalline solids in contrast to amorphous solids.

rubric.why: Amorphous solids lack long-range order and do not melt sharply.
rubric.description: States a structural or melting-point distinction for amorphous solids.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the irregular arrangement or gradual softening of amorphous solids.

modelAnswer: Crystalline solids have a regular, orderly arrangement of particles; amorphous solids have an irregular arrangement.
Crystalline solids have a sharp melting point; amorphous solids soften over a range of temperatures.

items.followUp: Define a supersaturated solution and state how it differs from a saturated solution.

rubric.why: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at that temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that no more solute can dissolve at the specified temperature.

rubric.why: An unsaturated solution contains less than the maximum and can dissolve more solute.
rubric.description: Distinguishes an unsaturated solution from a saturated one.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an unsaturated solution can still dissolve more solute at that temperature.

modelAnswer: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a specified temperature.
An unsaturated solution contains less than this maximum amount, so more solute can still dissolve at that temperature.

items.followUp: What is a suspension? Give two examples.

rubric.why: A true solution is a homogeneous mixture in which solute particles are uniformly distributed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing it as a homogeneous mixture of solute and solvent.

rubric.description: Gives two examples of true solutions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming any two valid examples, such as salt water and sugar water.

modelAnswer: A true solution is a homogeneous mixture in which the solute is uniformly distributed in the solvent.
Examples are salt water and sugar water.

items.followUp: Differentiate between exothermic and endothermic reactions.

rubric.why: A spontaneous reaction proceeds on its own under the stated conditions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it occurs on its own under the given conditions.

accept: does not occur on its own
rubric.why: A non-spontaneous reaction does not proceed on its own and needs an external input.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it requires an external energy supply or does not occur on its own under the given conditions.

modelAnswer: A spontaneous reaction occurs on its own under the given conditions without a continuous supply of external energy.
A non-spontaneous reaction does not occur on its own under the given conditions and requires an external energy supply.

items.followUp: Define a strong electrolyte and give two examples.

rubric.why: A weak electrolyte ionizes or dissociates only partially in solution and conducts electricity weakly.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it partially ionizes in aqueous solution or is a weak conductor because it produces few ions.

rubric.why: Acetic acid and ammonium hydroxide are examples of weak electrolytes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming two valid weak electrolytes.

modelAnswer: A weak electrolyte ionizes only partially in aqueous solution and is therefore a weak conductor of electricity.
Examples are acetic acid and ammonium hydroxide.

items.followUp: Why is the third ionization energy of aluminium much greater than its second ionization energy?

rubric.why: Magnesium loses its two outer 3s electrons in its first two ionizations.
rubric.description: Identifies the electron arrangement relevant to ionization.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that magnesium has two outer 3s electrons and that the first ionization removes one of them.

rubric.why: After the first ionization, the remaining electron is held more strongly by the positively charged ion, so removing it requires more energy.
rubric.description: Explains why the second ionization energy is higher.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the stronger attraction to the remaining electron in Mg+.

modelAnswer: A magnesium atom has two outer electrons in its 3s subshell; the first ionization removes one of them to form Mg+.
The remaining 3s electron is attracted more strongly by the positively charged Mg+ ion, so more energy is required to remove it in the second ionization.
